articles.title: 30 Months on the Exponential (in Charts)
articles.snippet: My second book on AI, Co-Existence, is out today (and you can get it here ), 30 months after the release of Co-Intelligence in early 2024. Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). It even caught that I’d gotten the math wrong. I was going to call this post “28 months on the exponential.” Some examples of interacting with Claude to make the graphics for this post. Notice that it corrected me. “This is the worst AI you will ever use” I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence , and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI. Which company had the best AI model in the world. But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone. We are living in an exponential The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. From the release of GPT-4 to the end of the METR measure, the amount of work AI could do doubled eight times. In 2024, an AI could do a four minute task. At the moment I turned in my draft of Co-Existence in April of 2026, an AI could do 17 hours of human work. And then the benchmark ran out. METR said they could no longer accurately measure the amount of work an AI could do using their current methods. Other studies suggest that number might be 17 weeks of work, or more. And, even as ability has increased, prices have dropped. My old favorite AI benchmark, the Google Proof Question and Answer Exam, which gives the AI problems that regularly stump graduate students, used to cost 30 cents in AI usage to get a single correct answer. Now, it costs four hundredths of a cent to get the same result. How humans work with AI is changing Despite all the progress, the frontier of AI ability is still jagged, just as it was 30 months ago. Some areas have stayed stubbornly weak (AI is still quite a bad long-form writer), while others, like solving math problems, went from terrible to superhuman in the same period. And, as I discuss in the book, even where AI is excellent, small gaps create large needs for humans, at least for now. But AI’s gains have been so large that how we work with it has to change. In Co-Intelligence , I wrote about centaur work (divided between AI and humans) and cyborg work (blended between AI and humans). Both keep you in the loop… but you can only be in so many loops at once. Now that we have real agents, I added a third way to work with AI: the conjurer. Conjurers summon agents when needed, assign them work, and evaluates what comes back. The charts in this post were made that way: I summoned agents, gave some general guidance, and I said “make it better” a lot. It is the most powerful way to use AI, and it carries new risks as we lose control over what, exactly, the AI is doing to get us those results. The Otter Test has fallen Regular readers will know that I have been testing AI image generation and movie tools with the prompt “Otter on an Airplane Using Wifi” for the past few years. This is what the best image generator, Midjourney, produced 30 months ago. So today I asked Opus 5.5 the following (typos and all, prompting has become much less important as AIs get better): “I have a post showing the what happened over the past 30 months of AI in honor of my new book (published 30 months after the origina). i want you to make the ultimate otter on an airplane using wifi video. just something fantastic, i know you are creative, give it a go.” Using my subscriptions to various online services from Google and ElevenLabs, it produced the following. (Turn the sound on) The video has a few flaws. But the AI figured out how to make it, from the script to the images to the concept to the music to the technical aspects of creating all of this, without any help from me. That is what has changed. This is the least we will ever talk about AI As a result of all of these gains, AI is only becoming a bigger issue in the world. articles.title: How to Stop Waiting and Start Living: A Jolt from Henry James
articles.snippet: “It wouldn’t have been failure to be bankrupt, dishonoured, pilloried, hanged; it was failure not to be anything.” “The things we want are transformative, and we don’t know or only think we know what is on the other side of that transformation,” Rebecca Solnit wrote in her exquisite Field Guide to Getting Lost . The wanting starts out innocently — awaiting the birthday, the new bicycle, Christmas morning; awaiting the school year to end, or to begin. Soon, we are awaiting the big break, the great love, the day we finally find ourselves — awaiting something or someone to deliver us from the tedium of life-as-it-is, into some other and more dazzling realm of life-as-it-could-be, all the while vacating the only sanctuary from the storm of uncertainty raging outside the frosted windows of the here and now. It matters not at all whether we are holding our breath for a triumph or bracing for a tragedy. For as long as we are waiting, we are not living. If we are not careful enough with the momentum of our own minds, we can live out our days in this expectant near-life existence. The Tiger by Franz Marc , 1912. (Available as a print and as stationery cards .) That is what Henry James (April 13, 1843–February 28, 1916) explores in his 1903 novella The Beast in the Jungle , found in his collection The Better Sort ( public library | public domain ) — the story of a man whose entire life, from his earliest memory, has been animated by “the sense of being kept for something rare and strange, possibly prodigious and terrible,” something fated “sooner or later to happen” and, in happening, to either destroy him or remake his life. He calls it “ the thing,” imagines it as a “beast in the jungle” lying in wait for him, and spends his life lying in wait for it, withholding his participation in the very experiences that might have that transformative effect — leaping after some great dream, risking his life for some great cause, falling in love. It is, of course, a dramatized caricature of our common curse — the treacherous “if only” mind that haunts all of us, in one way or another, to some degree or other, as we go through life expecting the next moment to contain what this one does not and, in granting us some mythic missing piece that forever keeps us from the warm glad feeling of enoughness, to render our lives worthy of having been lived. Art by Salvador Dalí for a rare 1946 edition of the essays of Montaigne James writes: Since it was in Time that he was to have met his fate, so it was in Time that his fate was to have acted; and as he waked up to the sense of no longer being young, which was exactly the sense of being stale, just as that, in turn, was the sense of being weak, he waked up to another matter beside. It all hung together; they were subject, he and the great vagueness, to an equal and indivisible law. When the possibilities themselves had accordingly turned stale, when the secret of the gods had grown faint, had perhaps even quite evaporated, that, and that only, was failure. It wouldn’t have been failure to be bankrupt, dishonoured, pilloried, hanged; it was failure not to be anything. When the protagonist meets a woman to whom his entire being pulls him, he begins spending time with her but ultimately keeps her heart at arm’s length, too afraid to love her, telling himself that he is protecting her from his fatalistic fate, failing to recognize that love itself is that great force of self-annihilation and transformation, “rare and strange” even as the most commonplace human experience. Discus chronologicus — a German depiction of time from the early 1720s. (Available as a print and as a wall clock .) When Time forecloses possibility, as Time always ultimately does, he arrives at his final reckoning at her tombstone: The escape would have been to love her; then, then he would have lived. She had lived — who could say now with what passion? — since she had loved him for himself… The Beast had lurked indeed, and the Beast, at its hour, had sprung; it had sprung in that twilight of the cold April when, pale, ill, wasted, but all beautiful, and perhaps even then recoverable, she had risen from her chair to stand before him and let him imaginably guess. It had sprung as he didn’t guess; it had sprung as she hopelessly turned from him, and the mark, by the time he left her, had fallen where it was to fall. He had justified his fear and achieved his fate; he had failed, with the last exactitude, of all he was to fail of; and a moan now rose to his lips… This was knowledge, knowledge under the breath of which the very tears in his eyes seemed to freeze. Through them, none the less, he tried to fix it and hold it; he kept it there before him so that he might feel the pain. That at least, belated and bitter, had something of the taste of life. But the bitterness suddenly sickened him, and it was as if, horribly, he saw, in the truth, in the cruelty of his image, what had been appointed and done. He saw the Jungle of his life and saw the lurking Beast; then, while he looked, perceived it, as by a stir of the air, rise, huge and hideous, for the leap that was to settle him. His eyes darkened — it was close; and, instinctively turning, in his hallucination, to avoid it, he flung himself, face down, on the tomb. Complement with Anaïs Nin on how reading awakens us from the trance of near-living and Mary Oliver on the key to living with maximum aliveness , then revisit Henry James’s equally brilliant sister Alice on how to live fully while dying . donating = loving For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). articles.title: Transcript: Bob Michele, CIO and Head of Global Fixed Income, Currency & Commodities, J.P. Morgan Asset Management
articles.snippet: The transcript from this week’s MiB: Bob Michele, CIO and Head of Global Fixed Income, Currency & Commodities, J.P. Morgan Asset Management , is below. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube , and Bloomberg . All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here . ~~~ Masters in Business Bob Michele, Chief Investment Officer and Head of Global Fixed Income, Currency and Commodities, J.P. Morgan Asset Management Bloomberg Radio | Transcript | October 2026 00:00:02 Bloomberg Audio Studios: podcasts, radio, news. 00:00:07 BARRY RITHOLTZ: This week on the podcast, another fantastic conversation. Bob Michele has had an amazing career. He could be one of the most informed, influential managers in the whole world of fixed income, in his perch as Chief Investment Officer and Head of Global Fixed Income, Currency and Commodities at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. He oversees a lot of assets and a lot of people, not just for corporate America and for central banks, but for regular investors, for pretty much everybody around the world. Few people know as much about what drives the fixed income markets as Bob does. I thought the conversation was fantastic, and I think you will also. With no further ado, my conversation with J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s Bob Michele. Bob Michele, welcome to Bloomberg. 00:01:12 BOB MICHELE: I’m thrilled to be here. 00:01:13 BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m thrilled to have you. The timing couldn’t be better. Before we talk about what you’ve built at J.P. Morgan and the state of the fixed income markets, I want to dive into your background, which is so interesting. University of Pennsylvania, classical languages degree. That is not the traditional route to managing fixed income. What was the original career plan? 00:01:41 BOB MICHELE: Well, it’s a good point. I’m here by accident, so that’s how the career plan worked out. Actually, I was a dual major. I also majored in natural sciences. Both my parents were doctors. My father was a surgeon, my mother was an orthodontist. Every job I had over the summer was pretty much working in a hospital or a lab somewhere. I was doing pre-med studies at Penn, ready to go to medical school. Unfortunately, my father died my junior year, and I decided maybe I should take a break before I do all of that. You’re at Penn, Wharton’s right there, everyone’s talking about business, going to work for a bank. And I said, why not me? I’ll do that for a year. Everyone laughed at me: You have absolutely no business courses. Give me one to take, I said, and they said, take accounting. So I took accounting second term my senior year, didn’t understand anything about it, interviewed with a load of banks, and someone was foolish enough to hire me: Bankers Trust. I’ll tell you, Barry, after one week in banking in New York City, I knew I was never going to medical school. 00:02:49 BARRY RITHOLTZ: Really? That’s fascinating. So it was just dumb luck. You ended up at Bankers Trust right out of college? 00:02:55 BOB MICHELE: Pretty much. I wrote to a lot of firms. I laugh, and maybe this is a complaint for the University of Pennsylvania. I went to College Hall and pulled Lehman out of the folder and sent them a letter. But Lehman was spelled L-E-G-H-M-A-N for some reason. So there was a typo. I didn’t know, right? I wasn’t a business major. I was doing sciences. I was doing classics, Latin and Greek. So I sent it off. They must have had a good laugh. I never heard back from them. 00:03:28 BARRY RITHOLTZ: Well, they assumed you were too risky, right? So you start on the investment management side at Bankers Trust as an analyst, eventually a portfolio manager. Then you shift to managing taxable and total return portfolios at Brown Brothers Harriman. You were never an economist, you were never a market strategist. You went straight from the classics to an analyst to a PM. Tell us about that progression. 00:03:58 BOB MICHELE: Well, there are a couple of things along the way that I learned. The first is I took the CFA. I figured if I didn’t have the background and the CFA was becoming popular, I could learn it. Then I also had a lot of confidence in myself. I sat there and I figured, if going to a class a couple of times a week for one term, you can learn organic chemistry, what if you’re doing something eight to 12 hours a day, five days a week, for 30 days? Can you learn it as quickly as you could organic chemistry? And the reality is, yeah, you could pick up a lot. You could teach yourself a lot. What did appeal to me was the mathematical aspect behind investments. Doing the sciences, there’s a lot of math involved, and there it is, right in investments. 00:04:53 BARRY RITHOLTZ: So people always bring up that it’s not a science, it’s not quite an art. It’s a little bit of a mix of both. Is the same true for fixed income? 00:05:04 BOB MICHELE: I think it’s a little bit more of a science than an art. Perhaps equities is a bit more art than science. I did a lot of equity work until the early nineties, and I switched purely to fixed income. And the attraction for me is the valuation metric that goes along with fixed income. You could model it. There was a maturity. All the dynamics behind the cash flows could be calculated. There was a finality to it that, to somebody with a math background, with a sciences background, was appealing. When I looked at the equity market, one of my early roommates in New York City, he and I would debate late in the evening about how do you value a stock. He was working in corporate finance at Bache at the time, and it would become very theoretical, and this would go on for a year, and we could never figure out what was the proper way to value a stock. There were dozens of ways, and every one of them seemed to be a different valuation. So I’m very happy with the choice I made. 00:06:09 BARRY RITHOLTZ: So you lead me to a really interesting recognit

articles.title: Avenda Health expands Unfold AI platform to support intraoperative prostate cancer care
articles.snippet: Unfold AI is designed to help physicians identify cancerous tissue. Source: Avenda Health Prostate treatment has improved with robotics, and it could improve again soon with artificial intelligence. Avenda Health today announced Surgery Mode, a new suit of interoperative features for its Unfold AI offering. The multimodal AI-powered prostate cancer mapping platform is designed to reveal the true size and extent of disease to help physicians make better informed treatment decisions. “Our goal with Unfold AI has always been to provide more clinical clarity throughout every stage of a patient’s cancer journey,” stated Shyam Natarajan, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Avenda Health . “Whether a physician is counseling a newly diagnosed patient, planning a targeted radiation oncology treatment, or performing a complex radical prostatectomy, having an accurate 3D map of the disease is transformative,” he added. “These new surgical enhancements empower physicians with the visual confidence needed to achieve optimal cancer control while protecting patient quality of life during complex procedures.” Founded in 2017, Avenda Health said it is creating a more personalized future of prostate cancer care. With deep learning, the Culver City, Calif.-based company ‘s software maps a patient’s cancer in 3D, giving physicians precise information and the confidence to make care decisions. Avenda said it aims to improve outcomes, preserve quality of life, and create a new standard of prostate cancer care. Avenda Health bases Surgery Mode on research Avenda Health said it designed Surgery Mode to enhance how surgeons use 3D AI mapping during non-robotic and robotic surgeries , alongside new tools to simplify patient case management and physician workflows. The launch builds on peer-reviewed research predicting that Unfold AI could cut positive surgical margins in half, substantially reducing cancer recurrence. In the study, the system outperformed MRI and other modalities in assessing whether cancer had spread beyond the prostate, assisting surgeons in making nerve-sparing decisions. In Surgery Mode, physicians can now access enlarged 3D views for clearer visualization, adjust the cancer estimation map to match the camera angle on the surgical console, review underlying MRI slices during the procedure, and access capsule risk scores from within a dedicated surgical view. Avenda Health claimed that Unfold AI is the only platform implementing multimodal AI to analyze a patient’s MRI, biopsy, pathology, and PSA together. It produces a personalized 3D map of the cancer’s extent to provide surgeons with more precise visualization of tumor boundaries. While Unfold AI has served as a decision-support tool during preoperative consultations, the latest expansion gives surgeons an enhanced version of these maps during prostate procedures. The suite of improved workflow tools also gives physicians and staff greater visibility into the status of each patient case. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! Key features Aligned Capsule Risk Score mapping: The Capsule Risk Score overlay now automatically flips its left/right visual orientation to mirror the surgical camera view, giving surgeons immediate, color-coded risk feedback by quadrant to guide precise nerve-sparing decisions in real time. Redesigned patient list and case filters: Improved patient organization and updated case status labels let users search for cases in progress, add new patients, and filter by status to see where each case stands at a glance. Improved administrative control: New built-in tools let staff verify insurance approvals and confirm administrative steps are complete before 3D map generation. Streamlined case management: Care teams can now add and view patient notes directly from the patient list and update the assigned physician on a patient report. Unfold AI helps doctors identify tumor extent Avenda Health said the expanded features extend Unfold AI’s reach across the prostate cancer care pathway, including active surveillance, focal therapy, surgical interventions, and radiotherapy. Its interactive 3D maps serve as a visual guide for patient counseling and decision support, helping patients and physicians confidently select their treatment path. Now, with Surgery Mode, the same patient-specific mapping technology can be used to provide clear visual boundaries in the operating room, actively guiding surgical procedures such as robotic prostatectomies. Unfold AI predicts the cancer’s spread into nearby anatomy with 92% accuracy , compared with 52% using MRI alone. That spatial clarity is central to helping surgeons determine whether a nerve-sparing or non-nerve-sparing surgery should be performed. Avenda noted that additional research demonstrated that Unfold AI improves physician identification of tumor extent , increasing sensitivity from 37% to 97%. By expanding Unfold AI from preoperative decision support into the operating room, the company said it is developing more precise views of prostate cancer that can support physicians across different stages of care. The post Avenda Health expands Unfold AI platform to support intraoperative prostate cancer care appeared first on The Robot Report .

articles.title: A guide to Day 1 of RoboBusiness 2026
articles.snippet: Today marks the start of RoboBusiness 2026! This year, we’ll be celebrating the 20th anniversary of RoboBusiness with the community that made it possible and looking ahead to more years of collaboration and growth. The event will start at the Santa Clara Convention Center at 9:15 a.m. PT with the opening keynote, “The Next 20 Years of Robotics.” As RoboBusiness marks its 20th anniversary, industry leaders will reflect on the breakthroughs that defined the past two decades and explore the technologies, markets, opportunities, and challenges that will shape the next 20 years. This year, all keynotes will take place in the theatre on the second floor. This talk will include Rodney Brooks, the co-founder and CTO of Robust AI ; Jonathan Hurst, the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics ; and Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley . At 10:00 a.m., the RoboBusiness show floor will open. articles.title: Gecko Robotics secures $300M contract with the U.S. Navy
articles.snippet: Gecko’s suite of technologies ensures data integrity by collecting and integrating full-coverage, high-fidelity data layers. | Source: Gecko Robotics Gecko Robotics this week said it has earned an additional $300 million its contract with the U.S. Navy and General Services Administration. With the increase, the U.S. Navy and GSA have quadrupled the ceiling value on Gecko’s contract for slashing maintenance delays and improving fleet readiness. The news came just six months after an initial $71 million IDIQ contract award. This fourfold expansion will accommodate rapid robotic deployment across the Navy and is one of the strongest public endorsements yet of operational AI and robotics in defense, claimed Gecko Robotics. The Pittsburgh-based company claimed that this showed the Pentagon’s confidence that it is delivering a core military capability of producing results, not experimental technology. “The conversation around AI and robotics in defense is no longer about experimental technology. It’s about delivering measurable and impactful returns,” said Jake Loosararian, co-founder and CEO of Gecko Robotics. “With savings of millions of dollars per ship, months of inspections turning into days, and warships returning to sea faster, the U.S. Navy is demonstrating to the world how to deploy technology at scale,” he added. “We’re proud to give our service members the tools they need to stay ahead of emerging threats.” Gecko said its AI and robotic technology can save the U.S. Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and return vessels to sea quicker. It does this by identifying structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods, reducing inspections from months to days. Komodo scans through deck coating without stripping them Central to the expansion is Komodo, a proprietary Gecko robotic technology system. Komodo scans through thick, non-skid deck coatings without stripping or damaging them, giving the Navy the ability to see the health of assets without taking it apart. It produces a full-deck heatmap of corrosion and material thickness, enabling repair teams to pinpoint damage and plan work before a ship enters drydock, which was previously possible only after maintenance had begun. The ceiling increase comes as the Department of the Navy places greater emphasis on fleet readiness as a national security priority. Each additional day a warship spends in maintenance reduces its ability to deter adversaries, respond to crises, and project power around the world, said the Navy. The chief of naval operations has set a target of 80% fleet readiness, which Gecko will have a crucial role in helping to meet. Gecko’s wall-climbing robots, drones, and fixed-sensors collect an unprecedented amount of data on the health of U.S. Navy ships and submarines, including components, hulls, decks and welds, with AI being used to create accurate models to identify any current and future structural issues, even ones that cannot be seen by the human eye. articles.title: Thieves’ cant slang
articles.snippet: Insider jargon, previously known as cant, is designed to keep outsiders out. The burglars in cartoons are often seen wearing a black mask over their eyes (like Robin in Batman but for a different reason) and carrying a bulging sack over their shoulders. [Of course, the burglar’s sack was rarely bulging. A robber would have to have the perfect haul to get the right mix of value, density and weight. You can’t fit a chest of drawers in the sack, and that much gold would be impossible to carry. But I digress.] The cant for this was ‘swag’, which comes from an old term for swaying or bulging. Sort of wishful thinking. And thus we get to the swag of business promo and conference loot… Establishing jargon is a key step in group identity. It’s rarely dictated from the top down, but permitting and celebrating it is a smart move if you’re looking for group cohesion.

articles.snippet: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. articles.title: Love After Life: Nobel-Winning Physicist Richard Feynman’s Extraordinary Letter to His Departed Wife
articles.snippet: Where the hard edge of physics meets the vulnerable metaphysics of the human heart. Few people have enchanted the popular imagination with science more powerfully and lastingly than physicist Richard Feynman (May 11, 1918–February 15, 1988) — the “Great Explainer” with the uncommon gift for bridging the essence of science with the most human and humane dimensions of life. Several months after Feynman’s death, while working on what would become Genius: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman ( public library ) — the masterly biography plumbing the wellspring of Feynman’s genius — James Gleick discovered something of arresting strangeness and splendor. “My heart stopped,” Gleick tells me. “I have never had an experience like that as a biographer, before or since.” In a mass of unread papers sent to him by Feynman’s widow, Gweneth, Gleick found a letter that discomposed his most central understanding of Feynman’s character. A generation after computing pioneer Alan Turing tussled with the binary code of body and spirit in the wake of loss , Feynman — a scientist perhaps uncommonly romantic yet resolutely rational and unsentimental in his reverence for the indomitable laws of physics that tend toward decay — penned a remarkable letter to a physical nonentity that was, for the future Nobel-winning physicist, the locus of an irrepressible metaphysical reality. Richard Feynman as a youth In high school, the teenage Richard spent summers at the beach in his native Far Rockaway. There, he grew besotted with a striking girl named Arline — a girl he knew he would marry. Both complement and counterpoint to his own nature, Arline met Richard’s inclination for science with ardor for philosophy and art. (The art class he took just to be near her would lay the foundation for his little-known, lifelong passion for drawing .) By his junior year, Richard proposed. Arline accepted. With the eyes of young love, they peered into a shared future of infinite possibility for bliss. Richard and Arline, 1940s But they were abruptly grounded when a mysterious malady began afflicting Arline with inexplicable symptoms — a lump would appear and disappear on her neck, fevers would roil over her with no apparent cause. Eventually, she was hospitalized for what was believed to be typhoid. Gleick writes: Feynman began to glimpse the special powerlessness that medical uncertainty can inflict on a scientific person. He had come to believe that the scientific way of thinking brought a measure of calmness and control in difficult situations — but not now. Just as Feynman began bombarding the doctors with questions that steered them toward a closer approximation of the scientific method, Arline began to recover just as mysteriously and unpredictably as she had fallen ill. But the respite was only temporary. The symptoms returned, still shorn of a concrete explanation but now unambiguously pointing toward the terminal — a prognosis Arline’s doctors kept from her. Richard refused to go along with the deception — he and Arline had promised each other to face life with unremitting truthfulness — but he was forced to calibrate his commitment to circumstance. Gleick writes: His parents, Arline’s parents, and the doctors all urged him not to be so cruel as to tell a young woman she was dying. His sister, Joan, sobbing, told him he was stubborn and heartless. He broke down and bowed to tradition. In her room at Farmingdale Hospital, with her parents at her side, he confirmed that she had glandular fever. Meanwhile, he started carrying around a letter — a “goodbye love letter,” as he called it — that he planned to give her when she discovered the truth. He was sure she would never forgive the unforgivable lie. He did not have long to wait. Soon after Arline returned home from the hospital she crept to the top of the stairs and overheard her mother weeping with a neighbor down in the kitchen. When she confronted Richard — his letter snug in his pocket — he told her the truth, handed her the letter, and asked her to marry him. Arline and Richard, 1940s Marriage, however, proved to be a towering practical problem — Princeton, where Feynman was now pursuing a Ph.D., threatened to withdraw the fellowships funding his graduate studies if he were to wed, for the university considered the emotional and pragmatic responsibilities of marriage a grave threat to academic discipline. Just as Feynman began considering leaving Princeton, a diagnosis detonated the situation — Arline had contracted a rare form of tuberculosis, most likely from unpasteurized milk. At first, Feynman was relieved that the grim alternative options of Hodgkin’s disease and incurable cancers like lymphoma had been ruled out. But he was underestimating, or perhaps misunderstanding, the gravity of tuberculosis — the very disease which had taken the love of Alan Turing’s life and which, during its two-century heyday, had claimed more lives around the globe than any other malady and all wars combined. At the time of Arline’s diagnosis in 1941, immunology was in its infancy, the antibiotic treatment of bacterial infections practically nonexistent, and the first successful medical application of penicillin a year away. Tuberculosis was a death sentence, even if it was a slow death with intervals of remission — a fact Richard and Arline faced with an ambivalent mix of brave lucidity and hope against hope. Meanwhile, Richard’s parents met the prospect of his marriage with bristling dread. His mother, who believed he was marrying Arline out of pity rather than love, admonished him that he would be putting his health and his very life in danger, and coldly worried about how the stigma attached to tuberculosis would impact her brilliant young son’s reputation. “I was surprised to learn such a marriage is not unlawful,” she scoffed unfeelingly. “It ought to be.” But Richard was buoyed by love — a love so large and luminous that he found himself singing aloud one day as he was arra

articles.title: New paper: Emerging trends in AI agent evaluation
articles.snippet: By Felix Chen, Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, and Arvind Narayanan. See the full author list and affiliations here . There are growing calls for independent and embedded AI evaluation, especially of AI agents. But much remains unclear: what constitutes a “good” evaluation, what needs to be evaluated in the first place, and how best to coordinate and support the influx of people entering the burgeoning evaluation ecosystem. Our group at Princeton has been working to improve the state of AI agent evaluation for about three years . We teamed up with people who’ve done foundational work on evaluation at Stanford, the UK AI Security Institute, and Brookings. Our paper is titled Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation. We synthesized the trends we see across three dimensions—the science and methods, the research agenda, and the evaluation ecosystem—with the goal to help those who are upskilling for this new paradigm. We also aim to equip evaluators, funders, and the public with a set of questions to ask, and provide actionable recommendations. Thirty-three emerging trends in AI agent evaluation. (Figure from the paper .) Challenges for agents, new and old AI developers have long made claims about the real-world performance of their systems based on benchmark scores. It is harder now to assess whether the evidence gathered supports claims made about agents. The evaluator must scrutinize the entire trajectory, not just the final outcome. It is important, for example, to know if agents took shortcuts, particularly since they have access to tools and environments. And when agents perform better or worse, it is harder to attribute these changes to different components of the agent. Addressing these concerns requires significant engineering effort, and the work is getting increasingly expensive—for example, several agents on the ExploitBench benchmark cost tens of thousands of dollars in credits to evaluate. These numbers also don’t factor in the significant engineering effort needed to set up and maintain the evaluation infrastructure itself. Agent evaluation is much more complex than model evaluation. (Figure from the paper .) Faced with the massive volume of traces that agents generate, evaluators are also struggling to inspect and monitor these agents at scale. The tools evaluators rely on today to do this work are not foolproof—and themselves require evaluation. To investigate the recent OpenAI-HuggingFace incident after the fact, evaluators relied upon other agents to look for and identify instances of harmful action, an approach they acknowledged carried its own limitations and biases. Because agents are deployed in dynamic settings (and increasingly together with other agents), it is harder to design good metrics to capture the underlying concepts of interest, and create valid conditions to implement them. Addressing these challenges will require better tools, more rigorous benchmarks, and experimentation with different approaches and formats, such as through open-world evaluations and growing observational data on real-world usage. The scope of evaluation needs is growing Evidence about agents is needed to understand their effects at different layers, but does not always translate across layers. (Figure from the paper .) Crucially, the results of evaluation at one level of scope are not guaranteed to translate to another. An agent might demonstrate capability in the lab, but face limits when placed in a specific use case. Consider METR’s randomized controlled trial which found that, despite expectations, usage of agent tools toward software development actually increased overall completion time on the tasks at hand. Agents may be able to perform certain tasks, but how that capability translates for humans in the real world requires evaluation in context. An expanded research agenda is therefore needed to understand agents at each level: their capabilities, their interactions with humans, and their impact on institutions and incentive structures. This work requires both technical and sociotechnical evaluation to study not just the agent itself but the agent(s) in context. Across these different layers, evaluators have a choice in framing the questions they ask and the findings they generate. Can an agent automate a task or process? Or, can an agent augment the work of a human? These are two complementary lenses. If evaluation largely focuses on how agents automate certain tasks, we will better understand where and how human work can be replaced. But it won’t tell us how humans can better collaborate using agents, or how agents can improve human work. Who gets to evaluate and how? This expanded research agenda will require an expanded set of evaluators from a mix of disciplines. It will also require that evaluators have the freedom to choose which questions to pursue and how. When evaluators with different approaches agree, we might gain greater confidence in those results. And when they conflict, evaluators can identify vague definitions and limitations to their findings. Who gets to participate, and with what independence, will shape the questions evaluators ask and the methods they use. Meaningful independence is influenced by several factors. As the costs of frontier evaluation keep increasing, the ability of independent evaluators to participate will be increasingly determined by their access to increased funding. Whether independent evaluators have sufficient access to models also impacts their ability to measure and assess the true frontier. Questions of access now also extend to Chain of Thought traces for agents, since frontier labs now release summarized versions instead of raw traces. Alongside these challenges, evaluators also need to navigate whether they can conduct work without fear of retaliation, and how they can transparently share their findings. Where do we go from here? articles.title: Daimon Robotics building the infrastructure layer for tactile intelligence
articles.snippet: Credit: Daimon Robotics Vision has become central to modern robotics, but cameras alone cannot tell a robot everything it needs to know about physical contact. When handling flexible objects, inserting components, or manipulating delicate items, robots need information about forces, slippage, and contact that visual systems may miss. Daimon Robotics wants to provide the infrastructure to help robots develop that capability. Rather than focusing exclusively on tactile sensors or developing a single foundation model, the company is building a pipeline that connects tactile sensing, data collection, simulation, and AI models. Its goal is to turn physical interactions into useful training data that helps robots perform manipulation tasks more reliably. “By building tactile intelligence, we’re actually playing the role as an infrastructure provider,” Daimon’s Partner & VP of Technology Dr. Zhu told The Robot Report . “We’re not aiming to be a foundation model developer. We are providing the infrastructure for doing so for those downstream customers.” That distinction is central to Daimon’s strategy: develop the tools and data infrastructure that other companies can use to build more capable robotic systems. Building a pipeline for tactile data Collecting useful tactile data at scale presents a challenge. Unlike visual data, which can be captured relatively easily with cameras, tactile data depends on physical contact. The resulting information varies with an object’s material, geometry, the forces applied, and the task being performed. Daimon is developing a pipeline to capture and process these interactions, with tactile feedback operating at 30 Hz. The company is also working to connect real-world data with simulation, allowing physical interactions to inform training in virtual environments. The sim-to-real gap remains a significant challenge, particularly when accurately reproducing physical properties such as friction and contact forces. Daimon’s approach starts by calibrating simulations against real-world measurements before transferring collected data into simulated environments. “Let’s be frank; it’s not good enough. It’s kind of terrible,” Zhu said of the current state of simulation, referring to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. Daimon is developing tactile simulations that account for physical properties measured through real-world testing. The goal is to improve the fidelity of those simulations and make it easier to transfer learned capabilities to physical robots. The company has discussed collecting more than 10,000 hours of data, with its longer-term Daimon-Infinity initiative targeting more than 1 million hours of tactile embodied data. Zhu also emphasized the importance of working with companies developing robotic models and applications. “Doing everything ourselves was not enough,” he said. “Collaborating internationally in different downstream scenarios is really important.” That collaboration helps Daimon understand what other developers need from its sensors, data-collection devices, software, and evaluation tools. Credit: Daimon Robotics From tactile demonstrations to industrial applications Daimon is targeting manipulation tasks such as assembly and packaging, where robots must respond to physical contact rather than simply follow predetermined trajectories. A robot might need to determine whether a component is properly seated, detect when an object slips, or adjust its movements when a part behaves unexpectedly. Tactile feedback can help it respond to these conditions. The company demonstrated applications involving delicate manipulation at IROS 2026, including applying heat-transfer designs to tote bags and threading bracelets. It also showed a robot collecting and packaging broken glass, illustrating how models trained on data from varied scenarios can be prompted to perform specific tasks. Daimon uses its Umi device to collect data from human interactions. Zhu said the company’s demonstrations were powered by foundation models trained on data collected across multiple scenarios, rather than being built solely around individual robot demonstrations. The company has identified Lenovo Capital and Inovance Technology as key partners. Zhu said Daimon has also moved beyond proof-of-concept projects into industrial assembly lines and warehouses, although he declined to name specific customers because of nondisclosure agreements. The commercial test is whether tactile sensing and the models built around it can improve performance consistently in production environments, where robots must handle variations in objects, materials, and operating conditions. Moving beyond visual perception Daimon’s broader strategy centers on developing models that can use tactile information to understand and respond to physical interactions. Its Daimon-TWM effort focuses on a tactile-grounded world model intended to help robots reason about physical interactions, rather than relying on visual perception alone. Recognizing an object is only part of manipulation. A robot must also understand how its actions affect that object and adjust when the physical result differs from expectations. Tactile feedback can help close that loop by providing information about contact and the consequences of an action. Zhu described two roles for tactile sensing in robotic systems: helping models reason about physical properties and enabling rapid adjustments during contact-intensive tasks. The latter can require high-frequency feedback, with Daimon targeting control at 30 Hz. The company is also exploring how data collected through human interactions can help train models for different robot configurations, including humanoids and dual-arm manipulators. But collecting data and training models are only part of the problem. Developers must still demonstrate that these systems generalize across different objects, materials, robots, and operating conditions. Scaling touch for robotics The bro

articles.title: Kodama raises $7M to bring robotics to forestry
articles.snippet: Kodama initially focused on wildfire risk reduction in the western U.S., but it is now focusing on the timber industry in the southeastern U.S. | Source: Kodama Kodama Systems today said it has raised $7 million to bring physical AI to forestry. The company said it will use the latest funding to support commercial deployments, deepen OEM partnerships, and continue development of supervised autonomy capabilities for complex off-road environments. “Right now, we’re working with different forestry companies across the southeastern U.S,” Ben Pinfield, a go-to-market associate at Kodama, told The Robot Report . “We’re at a point where we’re scaling, integrating into new machine types, and developing more autonomy capabilities in forestry .” Kodama’s technology is already deployed in commercial logging operations across the southeastern U.S. Over the past six months, machines equipped with the company’s technology have moved more than 100,000 tons of timber across multiple states. “We’re focused on specifically plantation timber operations,” said Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. “If we look more broadly, though, this is a tool for land management, and this is absolutely a tool that will be used in wildfire mitigation, from a forest thinning perspective, as well as wildfire suppression.” Including the latest funding, Kodama has raised a total of $14 million to date. Konvoy Ventures and Breakwater Ventures co-led the round. The round also included participation from Blue Forest Asset Management, NYA Ventures, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Congruent Ventures, Dangerous Ventures, M1C, and others. The forestry industry faces tough conditions Forest contractors are facing a lot of challenges. Demand for timber, forest management, and wildfire-resilience work is rising, but each requires long hours at remote job sites. “If you’re a 20-something-year-old prospective logger thinking about entering the industry, you need to be on-site at 5:30 a.m., which means you’re usually leaving your home at like 4:00 or 4:30 in the morning,” Jenkins said. “Then, you’re in a machine for nine or 10 hours a day, driving over stumps and rocks and through ruts, beating up your body all day long. There are some loggers that we’ve spoken with who have gone through, for example, eight skidder operators in a year. It’s brutal turnover in this industry for this type of operator.” As fewer people go into the industry and more operators retire, it’s getting harder and harder to find experienced, reliable operators, and fewer people want to get into the industry. “For the heavy equipment operations, that [work] can be pretty rough on their bodies,” Pinfield said. “It’s like the bang just isn’t worth the buck as far as the physical trade-off for a lot of these operators. So, our customers are having a hard time hiring talent. Even when they are able to hire talent, a lot of times, it’s unreliable.” What does Kodama’s technology do on job sites? Kodama says its technology is currently running 10 to 14 hours a day on work sites. | Source: Kodama Kodama combines supervised autonomy with teleoperation , enabling machines to handle repeatable tasks while experienced operators remotely manage complex work and edge cases. The Sonora, Calif.-based company said this hybrid approach amplifies the capabilities of skilled operators and improves machine utilization. Kodama said it is currently working with skidders on logging sites. “When a group of trees are cut down, a skidder with a big claw called the grapple picks them up, and drags them to the landing where they are then loaded into trucks. It’s essentially moving these trees from one place to another,” Pinfield explained. “The ultimate goal is also working on the other machines that are in those fleets, which are the cutter and the loader.” Kodama said as it deploys more machines, its data advantage compounds through a continuous learning loop across equipment, operators, worksites, and forestry workflows. “Every day that we remotely operate the machine, we’re generating about a terabyte of training data,” Jenkins said. “Starting two and a half years ago, we took the explicit direction of starting with teleoperation, and incrementally adding autonomy, versus autonomy first with a teleoperations failover. That’s been absolutely the right decision. Now the amount of training data that we are generating across different operating environments throughout the southeast is massive.” Kodama works directly with existing OEMs Merritt Jenkins, co-founder and CEO of Kodama. | Source: Kodama Kodama is building its platform within the existing forestry-equipment ecosystem. This allows customers to adopt new operating capabilities while preserving the value of their existing machine fleets. Jenkins said the company is integrated with two of the three largest equipment manufacturers in the world. “It’s preferable to integrate with the OEMs because you can leverage all of their knowledge and all of the sensors and fault detection that are already on the machine,” Jenkins said. Autonomy retrofits are common in the construction world, but these are typically after-market kits. Jenkins said in the construction space, OEMs like Caterpillar create closed systems, so it isn’t possible to collaborate directly with the OEM. Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! What has Kodama learned from job sites so far? Kodama has already had its technology deployed with customers in the southeast U.S. for the past two years. Pinfield said the company has been working with a customer in Georgia for over a year. “It’s always a learning process. Every logging site is a little bit different, with different terrain and a different crew that you have to work with and introduce this new technology to them,” Pinfield said. Among the biggest benefits of automation for these site operators are reliable and consistent operations. The team has also seen safety improvements with the technology. “

articles.title: The Long History of Underreporting Inflation
articles.snippet: It’s infuriating with each inflation print : Some economist or strategist waves off the hot headline number, advising you to focus on the core . The most recent bout of innumeracy has been going on for four years, but it dates back to at least the 2000s (and beyond). There is a long — and IMO, disgraceful — history of trying to underreport inflation data. Most people are unaware of it. This post will serve as a reminder that since World War Two, American governments have worked to reduce the reported inflation data—accuracy be damned. 1944-45: Mitchell Committee. Derives from the fight over wartime price controls and the Cost-of-Living Index (COLI). The legitimate accusation was that it understated wartime inflation as goods became unavailable, wages froze, and black-market pricing took over. COLI understated price increases by 4 percentage points from 1941–44. The BLS response: In 1945, the data series was renamed the “ Consumer Price Index ” and described as a fixed-basket price index. 1953: Postwar Basket Revisions. Comprehensive revisions rebuilt the goods basket from an earlier 1950 survey – the first since 1934–36. 1961: Stigler Committee. The Price Statistics Review Committee stated that CPI should be reconceived as a cost-of-living index. This included a series of well-intentioned changes (new-goods bias, quality change, substitution, along with hedonic adjustments).1 1972-75: Core Inflation. BLS’s “all items less food and energy” series dates back to 1957, but it was not a policy focus until the 1970s era of stagflation. After the 1972–73 food price spike, Fed Chair Arthur Burns had the Fed staff strip out food as “weather, not monetary policy”; then, after the embargo, energy was removed. Soon after, it was used cars, mobile homes, children’s toys, and so on until only a fraction of the basket remained. Hence, my 2005 phrase for this: “ Inflation Ex-Inflation . ” Over the ensuing decades, this was followed by the Cleveland Fed’s median/trimmed-mean CPI (1994), the Dallas Fed’s trimmed-mean PCE (2005), Atlanta’s sticky-price CPI (2010), and Powell’s “supercore” services ex housing (2022).2 The problem for consumers: You can’t eat core . 1983: Owners’ equivalent rent. The largest change in the basket, one with perverse, very counterintuitive results, especially leading up to the GFC and afterward. Before 1983, homeownership was an asset-price plus mortgage-interest cost. But mortgages hit 18% in 1981, causing the CPI to surge; 1980s COLAs were huge! BLS moved CPI-U to rental equivalence in January 1983; BEA’s PCE had used rental equivalence all along. It was a defensible concept; a house is an appreciating asset while shelter is a consumer good. But the 2002–07 housing bubble did not show up in CPI, because rent prices were restrained by millions of Americans stampeding into no-doc, ARM mortgage, home ownership purchases.3 We saw this OER distortion rear its head during the 2021–23 shelter price lag. 1995–96: Boskin Commission. Greenspan testified in Congressional testimony in January 1995 that CPI overstated inflation by 0.5–1.5 points.4 The Commission (Boskin, Dulberger, Gordon, Griliches, Jorgenson) reported in December 1996 that there was an upward bias of 1.1 points a year, with a range 0.8–1.6.5 It was pure political bullshit . The political purpose was to reduce COLA and tax bracket creep, saving $1 trillion dollar deficit reduction over the next decade or so. BLS implemented it administratively. In “Bailout Nation,” I discuss the role this stealth inflation played in the crisis.6 Here was my question in the 2000s: If inflation was properly reported (e.g., pre-Boskin), might the Federal Reserve have picked up the distortions in the backward, real estate-driven economy? 2017: Chained CPI as fiscal policy. It’s ironic that the only Obama policy idea adopted by Trump was the proposed C-CPI-U for Social Security COLAs and tax indexing. It was implemented in the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.7 2000: Fed changes its target to PCE. February 2000 Monetary Policy Report shifted the Fed’s preferred gauge from CPI to PCE (broader scope, chained formula, business-survey weights including 3rd-party health spending); 2004: Fed changes its target to Core PCE . Since 2012, the 2% target is a PCE target. This lowered the inflation number the Fed is judged against by ~0.5 pts/yr versus CPI. 2020–26: Annualizing. Weights moved to annual updates in 2023, a response to the pandemic basket shock. By October 2023, this created reporting issues: a health-insurance smoothing fix, a 2022 new-tenant rent index to address shelter lag, and in 2025 BLS replaced survey collection with vendor transaction data for leased vehicles (April 2025) and wireless services (July 2025), 2025: Suspending CPI . DOGE firing and other staffing cuts led BLS to suspend CPI collection in several metro areas in 2025; it was replaced with (LOL) imputation. Trump fired Commissioner McEntarfer on August 1, 2025, after a bad jobs report, and the Antoni nomination that followed did not go through. The 2025 episode is something brand new, different, and much worse : not creatively re-measuring inflation downwards, but ceasing to measure it entirely.8 ~~~ It is no coincidence: Every major change since 1983 went in the same direction – reducing the reporting of inflation data, regardless of increasing prices, often with dire consequences. Technical changes in the US have been nearly all directional in the same way, and almost always timed to a fiscal or political need. articles.title: The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build
articles.snippet: Agility Robotics , the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5 . It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do. Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined. From ATRIAS to Digit My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals. We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS —short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait. With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be? Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones , and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie . Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them. ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year. Agility Robotics Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash. Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1 , which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers. Why Digit Began With Warehouse Bins As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers. After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins . Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. articles.title: When Relationships Change: Anne Morrow Lindbergh on Embracing the Intermittency and Mutability of Love
articles.snippet: “All living relationships are in process of change, of expansion, and must perpetually be building themselves new forms.” “God is Change,” Octavia Butler wrote , channeling in poetic truth the fundamental scientific fact of the universe . We know this. And yet to be human is to long for constancy, to crave the touchingly impossible assurance that what we have and cherish will be ours to hold forever, just as it is now. We build homes — fragile haikus of concrete and glass to be unwritten by the first earthquake or flood. We make vows — fragile promises to be upheld by selves we haven’t met in a future we can’t predict. The dearer we hold something, the more tightly we cling to the dream of constancy, the more zealously we torture ourselves with the belief that any change is loss. Naturally, it is in our intimate relationships that we most come to fear change and most suffer when it comes — a fear not at all groundless, given what relationship rupture does to our limbic system . The salve for this singularly discomposing suffering comes not from ossifying change but from changing our beliefs about it. Such salutary recalibration is what the aviator and writer Anne Morrow Lindbergh (June 22, 1906–February 7, 2001) offers in Gift from the Sea ( public library ) — a book I found in a Little Free Library and felt immediately speaking to my soul, drawn from the diaries Lindbergh kept during two weeks of solitude on the ocean shore “searching for a new pattern of living” as she was entering the second half of her life, that vital “period of second flowering” when one is “free for growth of mind, heart and talent.” Anne Morrow Lindbergh Reflecting on the natural trajectory of intimate relationships, she writes: The pure relationship, how beautiful it is! How easily it is damaged, or weighed down with irrelevancies — not even irrelevancies, just life itself, the accumulations of life and of time. For the first part of every relationship is pure, whether it be with friend or lover, husband or child. It is pure, simple and unencumbered. It is like the artist’s vision before he has to discipline it into form, or like the flower of love before it has ripened to the firm but heavy fruit of responsibility. Every relationship seems simple at its start. The simplicity of first love, or friendliness, the mutuality of first sympathy seems, at its initial appearance — even if merely in exciting conversation across a dinner table — to be a self-enclosed world. Two people listening to each other, two shells meeting each other, making one world between them… It is free of ties or claims, unburdened by responsibilities, by worry about the future or debts to the past. And then how swiftly, how inevitably the perfect unity is invaded; the relationship changes; it becomes complicated, encumbered by its contact with the world. While this is true in most relationships, Lindbergh observes, the pattern is most pronounced — and most painful — in our most intimate bonds. And yet the pain we experience as a relationship exits this early stage of unselfconscious mutual elation is not evidence of loss — it is evidence of our misshapen ideals of closeness as a static pattern of attachment. She offers an alternative orientation to the inevitability of change: We mistakenly feel that failure to maintain its exact original pattern is tragedy. It is true, of course, the original relationship is very beautiful. Its self-enclosed perfection wears the freshness of a spring morning. Forgetting about the summer to come, one often feels one would like to prolong the spring of early love, when two people stand as individuals, without past or future, facing each other. One resents any change, even though one knows that transformation is natural and part of the process of life and its evolution. Like its parallel in physical passion, the early ecstatic stage of a relationship cannot continue always at the same pitch of intensity. It moves to another phase of growth which one should not dread, but welcome as one welcomes summer after spring. Art from Bunny & Tree by Balint Zsako At the heart of this dread is our unwillingness to relinquish the polished self-image we see in the light-filled eyes of the other in those early stages of mutual infatuation, before we have touched each other’s darkness, before we have met the hungry ghosts of each other’s unmet needs. We long for that image, perfect and haloed with adoration, to become our identity, seeking to make of love a flattering mirror in which to find our best selves, tasking the other with the emotional brunt of bearing the parts we don’t want to look at. Lindbergh pulls back the curtain on the most damaging myth handed down to us by the Romantics: Certainly, one has the illusion that one will find oneself in being loved for what one really is, not for a collection of functions. But can one actually find oneself in someone else? In someone else’s love? Or even in the mirror someone else holds up for one? I believe that true identity is found… in creative activity springing from within. It is found, paradoxically, when one loses oneself. One must lose one’s life to find it… Only a refound person can refind a personal relationship. The twin root of our suffering in a changing relationship is the expectation — the demand, even — that the other’s love be total and permanent, reserved for us alone, unshared with other priorities and passions, those natural constituents of a fully developed personality and a fully inhabited life. Lindbergh writes: We all wish to be loved alone… Perhaps, as Auden says in his poem, this is a fundamental error in mankind. For the error bred in the bone Of each woman and each man Craves what it cannot have, Not universal love But to be loved alone. Lindbergh recounts discussing this verse with an Indian philosopher, who made a striking observation — while mutuality is the essence of love and therefore it is natural for us to wish for it, it is in the time-

articles.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
articles.snippet: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech – some of which was ad libbed and not captured here – I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress. Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership. *** Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here. To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials later. My whole career has been defined by finding information that seemed important to the future of the world, then telling the world about that information.Two decades ago, I started my career as a journalist, focusing on data centers. Through that work, I became so obsessed with AI that in 2016 I left journalism to work at OpenAI, then co-founded Anthropic a few years later. Ever since, I’ve been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet, and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves. Well, the moment has arrived. AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world – as we’ve heard in so many sessions here – and is contributing to its own development. Of course, many of you know this, and you are having to track AI as one of a multitude of destabilizing forces that is shaping your world and your work. What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly. And I’m going to explain why. For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up. They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun. The writer Vernor Vinge forecast this in 1993. “When greater-than-human intelligence drives progress, that progress will be much more rapid. In fact, there seems no reason why progress itself would not involve the creation of still more intelligent entities — on a still-shorter time scale,” he wrote, describing the singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” The singularity is here . The implications reach across every aspect of life. But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. This will feel confusing and disorienting, and it will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril. Today, I’m going to concentrate on the first point: the potential benefits of rapid AI progress, and what we need to do to share in these benefits together. So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. I believe that AI-driven scientific invention will change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones, and –– at the same time –– cause us all to ask deep philosophical questions about choices we should make about its continued development. I’ll develop my claim: For the last half century, most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly – ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find. But something important has changed: we’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor. This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers. As a consequence, the field of software development is changing – A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans. We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life. But new AI capabilities bring new challenges – the coding improvements have meant AI systems have got much better at cybersecurity and cyberattacks –– leading the world to race to deploy these p
